title: RD-HRL: Generating Reliable Sub-Goals for Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Tasks
claim: Value-based subgoal selection is unreliable: generalization noise in Bellman backups steers planners toward sub-optimal trajectories even when optimal sub-trajectories exist in the data.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right on maze grids, shared legend on top, check/cross badges
description: A shared legend runs across the top: goal pin, current-state diamond, small circles for states, dashed transition regions, orange dotted sub-optimal trajectory, blue dotted optimal trajectory, and dark green and light green Bellman-backup arrows. Below are three identical grey maze maps. (a) shows the offline dataset: two orange trajectories τ1 and τ2 from start s_t to goal g, which cross at a transition region z. (b) shows the ideal outcome, a blue dotted optimal path that follows the first part of τ1 and then the end of τ2, marked with a blue check. (c) shows the failure: Bellman backups from the goal, including a light generalized one, favor the sub-optimal orange route, marked with an orange cross. Orange and blue contrast the bad and good outcomes.
caption: The dataset contains two trajectories, τ1 and τ2, as is shown in (a). Note that, τ2 successfully reached the goal point g, yet τ2 contains a sub-optimal sub-trajectory; meanwhile, τ1 fails to reach the goal, but τ1 provides an optimal sub-trajectory from st to s1
abstract: Long-horizon sparse-reward tasks, such as goal-conditioned or robot manipulation tasks, remain challenging in offline reinforcement learning due to the credit assignment problem. Hierarchical methods have been proposed to tackle this problem by introducing sub-goal planning guided by value functions, which in principle can shorten the effective planning horizon for both high-level and low-level planners, and thereby avoiding the credit assignment problem. However, we demonstrate that the sub-goal selection mechanism is unreliable, as it relies on value functions suffering from generalization noise, which misguides value estimation and thus leads to sub-optimal sub-goals. In this work, to provide more reliable sub-goals, we novelly introduce a reliability-driven decision mechanism, and propose Reliability-Driven HRL (RD-HRL) as the solution. The reliability-driven decision mechanism provide decision-level targets for high-level policy, thereby providing noise-immune decision spaces for them, ensuring the reliability of sub-goals (which are termed as action-level targets in this paper). Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach RD-HRL outperforms baseline methods across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the competitive advantages of RD-HRL. Our code is anonymously available at \url{https://github.com/Looomo/RD-HRL-public}.
